verse.text: Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy, to the assembly of the Thessalonians in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ: Grace to you and peace.
verse.note: The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering and, in the Greek Old Testament, for Israel assembled before God. 'Church' is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. 'Assembly' is used throughout this translation so that the one Greek word is visible as one word.

note.traditional: Grace be unto you, and peace, from God our Father, and the Lord Jesus Christ.

verse.note: Many later manuscripts add 'from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ', matching the greeting in Paul's other letters. The earliest witnesses have the short form, and the longer one is generally regarded as a scribal harmonisation.

verse.text: We always give thanks to God for all of you, making mention of you in our prayers, constantly
verse.note: The adverb stands at the boundary between two clauses and can be read with either: 'mentioning you constantly in our prayers' or 'constantly remembering your work'. The edition translated here punctuates it with what follows, and the translation does the same; the sense differs little.

verse.text: remembering your work of faith, your labor of love, and your endurance of hope in our Lord Jesus Christ, in the presence of our God and Father,

note.term: in the presence of our God and Father
note.traditional: in the sight of God and our Father

verse.note: The phrase comes at the end of the Greek sentence and may describe where Paul does his remembering (in prayer before God) or where the Thessalonians' faith, love and hope are lived out. The translation leaves it at the end so that either reading remains possible. The three paired nouns are most often understood as work that springs from faith, labor prompted by love, and endurance sustained by hope.

verse.text: knowing, brothers and sisters loved by God, that he has chosen you,
verse.note: The Greek plural was the normal way to address a mixed group of men and women as siblings, and the letter is written to the whole community. Older translations have 'brethren' or 'brothers'; many recent ones use 'brothers and sisters', as here.

verse.text: because our good news did not come to you in word alone, but also in power and in the Holy Spirit and with great conviction, just as you know what kind of people we were among you for your sake.
verse.note: The Greek conjunction can mean 'because', giving the grounds on which Paul knows God has chosen them, or 'that', spelling out what the choosing consisted of. Most interpreters take it as 'because', and the translation follows them.

The word meant an announcement of good news, used in the period for public tidings such as a victory or a ruler's accession, and in the Greek Old Testament for news of God's deliverance. 'Gospel' is the traditional rendering and remains common, but it now suggests a book or a body of doctrine. Several modern translations also use 'good news'.

The noun can mean full assurance or certainty, and some take it as 'fullness'. It probably describes the confidence with which the missionaries preached, since the sentence goes on to speak of their conduct, though some refer it to the conviction produced in the hearers.

verse.text: And you became imitators of us and of the Lord, receiving the word in great affliction with joy from the Holy Spirit,
so that you became an example to all who believe in Macedonia and in Achaia.
verse.note: These were the two Roman provinces that together covered most of Greece: Macedonia in the north, with Thessalonica as its chief city, and Achaia in the south, including Corinth and Athens. Paul is most likely writing from Corinth, in Achaia.

verse.text: For from you the word of the Lord has rung out, not only in Macedonia and Achaia, but in every place your faith toward God has gone out, so that we have no need to say anything.
For they themselves report about us what kind of entrance we had among you, and how you turned to God from idols, to serve a living and true God

note.term: what kind of entrance we had among you
note.traditional: what manner of entering in we had unto you

verse.note: The noun means an entering or arrival. Many translations render it 'welcome' or 'reception', focusing on how the Thessalonians received the missionaries; others take it as the character of the visit itself, which is how the word is used again at the start of the next chapter. 'Entrance' leaves both open.

verse.text: and to wait for his Son from the heavens, whom he raised from the dead: Jesus, who rescues us from the coming wrath.
verse.note: The Greek is plural, a Semitic turn of phrase carried over from Hebrew through the Greek Old Testament. Most translations flatten it to 'heaven'; the plural is kept here wherever the Greek has it and God's dwelling is meant.

verse.text: For you yourselves know, brothers and sisters, that our visit to you has not proved empty,
verse.note: The Greek plural was the ordinary way to address a mixed group of men and women as siblings, and Paul is writing to the whole community. 'Brothers' alone now suggests to English readers that only men are addressed. Many recent translations make the same choice.

The word can mean 'without result' (the traditional 'in vain') or 'without substance', that is, hollow or insincere. Because the verses that follow defend the missionaries' character and motives and not their success, many scholars prefer the second sense. 'Empty' leaves both open, as the Greek does.

verse.text: but though we had already suffered and been shamefully treated in Philippi, as you know, we found boldness in our God to speak to you the good news of God amid a great struggle.
verse.note: The Greek was an ordinary word for an announcement of good news, used also of public and imperial proclamations. 'Gospel' has become a purely religious term and a book title, so the plain meaning is given here. Many modern translations alternate between the two.

verse.text: For our appeal does not come from error or from impurity, nor is it made with deceit,
but just as we have been tested and found fit by God to be entrusted with the good news, so we speak, not to please people but to please God, who tests our hearts.
For we never came with flattering speech, as you know, nor with a pretext for greed—God is witness—
nor did we seek glory from people, whether from you or from others,
though as apostles of Christ we could have made our weight felt. But we were gentle among you, like a nurse cherishing her own children.
verse.note: The Greek says literally 'to be in weight'. It may mean being a financial burden, as the related verb in verse 9 does, or carrying weight in the sense of insisting on one's authority and importance. Scholars are divided, and Paul may intend both. The rendering keeps 'weight' so that the link with verse 9 remains visible.

Manuscripts are split between 'gentle' (ēpioi) and 'infants' (nēpioi), which differ by a single letter. The edition translated here reads 'gentle', as do most English versions. Many of the earliest manuscripts read 'infants', and some critical editions and scholars prefer that reading as the harder one.

The word usually denotes a wet nurse, a woman employed to suckle and raise another family's children, and a familiar figure of affection in ancient households. The point of 'her own children' is probably that even a professional nurse shows a special tenderness when the children are hers. Some translations simplify to 'nursing mother'.

verse.text: Longing for you so, we were glad to share with you not only the good news of God but our own lives as well, because you had become dear to us.
For you remember, brothers and sisters, our labor and toil: working night and day so as not to weigh on any of you, we proclaimed to you the good news of God.
You are witnesses, and so is God, how devoutly and justly and blamelessly we behaved toward you who believe,
verse.note: Greek has a single word-family where English has two: righteous and just, righteousness and justice. The adverb here belongs to that family and describes conduct that is in the right before God and fair toward others.

verse.text: just as you know how we treated each one of you as a father treats his own children,
appealing to you, encouraging you, and solemnly charging you to walk in a way worthy of God, who calls you into his own kingdom and glory.

And for this reason we too thank God unceasingly: when you received the word of God that you heard from us, you accepted it not as the word of people but as what it truly is, the word of God, which is also at work in you who believe.

For you, brothers and sisters, became imitators of the assemblies of God in Christ Jesus that are in Judea, because you too suffered the same things from your own compatriots as they did from the Jews
verse.note: The Greek word meant a gathering of citizens and, in the Greek Scriptures, the assembled people of Israel. 'Church' now suggests a building or an institution, neither of which existed yet. 'Church' is the near-universal rendering, and readers should understand the same communities by 'assembly'.

note.traditional: the Jews, who killed the Lord Jesus

verse.note: Greek manuscripts have no punctuation here. Most translations place a comma after 'Jews', making what follows a description of the Jewish people as a whole. The Greek construction more naturally identifies a particular group, those who did these things, and the text is rendered that way without a comma. Paul and the Judean assemblies were themselves Jews, and since the setting is Judea some scholars translate 'Judeans'.

verse.text: who killed both the Lord Jesus and the prophets and drove us out, who do not please God and are opposed to all people,
preventing us from speaking to the Gentiles so that they may be saved, so as always to fill up the measure of their sins. But the wrath has come upon them at last.
verse.note: The Greek word means 'peoples' or 'nations'. In the plural, Jewish writers used it for all the non-Jewish peoples. English uses 'Gentiles' for that sense and 'nations' elsewhere, but it is one word in Greek.

The phrase can mean 'at last', 'completely' or 'to the end, forever', and translations differ. It is also uncertain what event Paul has in mind, or whether he speaks of a future judgment as so certain that it is already present. A minority of scholars regard verses 13–16 as a later addition, though all manuscripts contain them.

verse.text: But we, brothers and sisters, orphaned from you for a short time—in person, not in heart—tried all the harder, with great desire, to see you face to face.
For we wanted to come to you—I, Paul, more than once—but Satan blocked us.
For what is our hope or joy or crown to boast of before our Lord Jesus at his coming? Is it not you?
verse.note: The word means arrival and the presence that follows. In Paul's day it was a standard term for the state visit of a king or emperor to a city, an occasion for celebration and for honours such as crowns. That association fits the crown imagery in this verse.

verse.text: Yes, you are our glory and our joy.
So when we could bear it no longer, we decided to be left behind in Athens alone,
verse.note: The Greek 'we' and 'alone' are plural. This may be a literary plural meaning Paul by himself (compare 'I sent' in verse 5), or it may include Silvanus, who is named with Paul as a sender of the letter. Scholars are divided, and the translation keeps the plural without deciding.

verse.text: and we sent Timothy, our brother and God's coworker in the good news of Christ, to strengthen and encourage you for the sake of your faith,

note.traditional: minister of God / our fellow labourer

verse.note: Manuscripts differ here: some read 'God's servant', some simply 'coworker', and some combine the two. Most scholars think 'God's coworker' is original and that copyists softened a phrase that seemed too bold. It can mean one who works alongside God or a colleague of Paul's in God's service; 1 Corinthians 3:9 uses the same expression.

The traditional 'gospel' has become a religious term, but the Greek word was the ordinary one for an announcement of good news, such as a victory. Rendering it this way also preserves a link with verse 6, where Paul uses the related verb, elsewhere his word for proclaiming the message about Christ, for Timothy's good report about the Thessalonians. Many modern translations alternate between 'gospel' and 'good news'.

verse.text: so that no one would be shaken amid these afflictions. For you yourselves know that this is what we are appointed for.
verse.note: This verb occurs only here in the New Testament. Its older sense is of a dog wagging its tail, and from that 'to fawn on' or 'to beguile', so some take the meaning to be 'so that no one would be lured away'. Most translators and the ancient versions understand it as 'shaken' or 'unsettled', which is followed here.

verse.text: Indeed, when we were with you, we kept telling you in advance that we were going to suffer affliction, and so it happened, as you know.
That is why, when I too could bear it no longer, I sent to find out about your faith, for fear that the tempter had somehow tempted you and our labor would turn out to be for nothing.

note.term: the tempter had somehow tempted you

verse.note: The Greek verb covers both 'tempt' and 'put to the test', and the title and the verb are the same word. Here the testing is the pressure of persecution, which might lead the Thessalonians to abandon their faith. 'The tempter' is Satan, named in 2:18.

verse.text: But just now Timothy has come to us from you and brought us the good news of your faith and love. He has told us that you always remember us fondly and long to see us, just as we long to see you.
Because of this, brothers and sisters, in all our distress and affliction we were encouraged about you through your faith,
verse.note: The Greek plural was the normal way to address a mixed group of men and women as siblings, and Paul is writing to the whole congregation. 'Brothers' alone would suggest to a modern reader that only men are addressed. Many recent translations make the same choice.

verse.text: for now we live, if you are standing firm in the Lord.
For what thanks can we give back to God for you, for all the joy with which we rejoice because of you before our God,
as night and day we pray with the utmost earnestness to see your face and to make good what is lacking in your faith?
Now may our God and Father himself, and our Lord Jesus, direct our way to you.
verse.note: The verb is singular in Greek although it has two subjects, God the Father and the Lord Jesus. Greek sometimes lets a verb agree with only one of a pair of subjects, so the grammar alone proves little. Many interpreters nonetheless note how closely Paul joins the two in a single prayer. The verb means to make a road straight, answering the obstruction mentioned in 2:18.

verse.text: And as for you, may the Lord make you increase and overflow in love for one another and for everyone, just as we do for you,
so as to strengthen your hearts to be blameless in holiness before our God and Father at the coming of our Lord Jesus with all his holy ones.
verse.note: The Greek word means arrival and the presence that follows. It was the regular term for the official visit of a king or emperor to a city. Paul uses it for the expected arrival of Jesus as Lord.

'Saints' now suggests canonised individuals or people of exceptional virtue, whereas the Greek simply means those who are holy, set apart for God. Paul normally uses it of believers, but here many scholars think he means angels accompanying the Lord, echoing Zechariah 14:5 ('the Lord my God will come, and all the holy ones with him'). 'Holy ones' leaves both readings open.

Some important manuscripts add 'Amen' at the end of this verse. The edition translated here omits it, judging it more likely that copyists added the word to a prayer than that they removed it. The question remains open.

verse.text: Finally then, brothers and sisters, we ask and urge you in the Lord Jesus that, just as you received from us how you must walk and please God—as indeed you are walking—you do so more and more.
verse.note: The Greek masculine plural was the ordinary way to address a mixed group, and Paul is writing to the whole congregation. Many recent translations render it this way; others keep “brothers” and explain in a footnote. The singular in verse 6 is rendered “a brother or sister” on the same basis, though some interpreters think a male fellow believer is specifically in view there.

verse.text: For you know what instructions we gave you through the Lord Jesus.
For this is God's will, your holiness: that you keep away from sexual immorality;
verse.note: The word denotes being set apart for God and the way of life that follows from it. “Sanctification” has since become a technical term of theology, which the first readers would not have heard. “Holiness” also keeps visible the link Paul draws with the “Holy” Spirit in verse 8. Modern translations vary between the two.

verse.text: that each of you know how to gain control of your own body in holiness and honor,

note.term: gain control of your own body

verse.note: The Greek is literally “acquire (or possess) his own vessel.” “Vessel” is a metaphor, and interpreters ancient and modern are divided on whether it means one's own body or one's wife. On the second reading the sense is “take a wife for himself in holiness and honor.” The verb normally means “acquire,” which favours “wife”; “vessel” as an image for the body is the better-attested usage. Most recent translations choose “body,” but the question remains open.

verse.text: not in lustful passion like the Gentiles who do not know God;
verse.note: The same Greek word means “nations” or “peoples” and, in Jewish usage, the non-Jewish peoples in particular; this translation renders it by sense. Most of the Thessalonian believers were themselves non-Jews by birth. Paul nevertheless uses the word for outsiders who do not know God, placing his readers on the other side of that line.

verse.text: that no one overstep the bounds and take advantage of a brother or sister in this matter, because the Lord is an avenger in all these things, just as we told you before and solemnly warned you.

note.traditional: in any matter / in this matter

verse.note: The word can mean a business dealing, and some read the verse as a new topic: not cheating a fellow believer in commerce. The definite article and the surrounding verses on sexual conduct lead most scholars to take it as “the matter” under discussion, so that the wrong in view is sexual, such as adultery that violates another person's household.

verse.text: For God did not call us to impurity but in holiness.
So then, whoever rejects this is rejecting not a human being but God, who indeed gives his Holy Spirit to you.
Now about love for your brothers and sisters, you do not need anyone to write to you, for you yourselves are taught by God to love one another;

note.term: love for your brothers and sisters

verse.note: In ordinary Greek this word normally meant affection between actual siblings. Paul applies it to the members of the congregation, treating them as a family. The phrase “taught by God” translates a single compound word that is not found before Paul and may be his own coinage.

verse.text: and indeed you are doing this toward all the brothers and sisters throughout Macedonia. But we urge you, brothers and sisters, to do so more and more,
and to make it your ambition to live quietly, to mind your own affairs, and to work with your hands, just as we instructed you,
so that you may walk decently toward outsiders and have need of no one.
We do not want you to be uninformed, brothers and sisters, about those who are asleep, so that you will not grieve as the rest do, who have no hope.
verse.note: Sleep was a common euphemism for death in both Greek and Jewish usage, and the word alone does not settle any question about the state of the dead. Some translations render it plainly as “those who have died.” The metaphor is kept here because Paul uses the plain word “the dead” separately in verse 16.

verse.text: For if we believe that Jesus died and rose, then in the same way through Jesus God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep.

note.traditional: them also which sleep in Jesus

verse.note: In the Greek, “through Jesus” stands between “those who have fallen asleep” and “will bring,” and can attach to either. The older tradition reads “those who have fallen asleep through Jesus,” meaning those who died as his people. Many recent translations, as here, take it with the verb: God will bring them through Jesus' agency. Both readings have scholarly support.

verse.text: For this we tell you by a word of the Lord: we who are alive, who are left until the coming of the Lord, will certainly not go ahead of those who have fallen asleep.

note.term: by a word of the Lord
note.traditional: by the word of the Lord

verse.note: Paul claims the Lord's authority for what follows, but it is disputed what he means. He may mean a saying of Jesus handed down in the tradition, whether or not it is preserved in the Gospels. Or he may mean a revelation given through a Christian prophet, possibly Paul himself. The phrase echoes the Septuagint's language for prophetic messages.

The word means arrival and the presence that follows. In the period it was a regular term for the official visit of a king, emperor or high official to a city. Readers in a provincial city such as Thessalonica would have known that usage. Its sense is therefore fuller than the plain English “coming” suggests.

verse.text: For the Lord himself, with a shout of command, with an archangel's voice and with God's trumpet, will come down from heaven, and the dead in Christ will rise first.
Then we who are alive, who are left, will be snatched up together with them in clouds to meet the Lord in the air; and so we will always be with the Lord.
verse.note: The verb means to seize or carry off suddenly and by force; it is used of robbers, wild animals and abductions. “Caught up” is accurate but has become mild with familiarity. The Latin translation of this word is the source of the English term “rapture.”

The Greek noun was often used for a city's delegation going out to welcome an arriving dignitary and escort him back in. Many scholars think Paul draws on that picture here, which would imply that those who meet the Lord accompany him on his arrival and are not taken away. Others doubt that the word is a technical term, and the text does not say what happens after the meeting.

verse.text: So then, encourage one another with these words.
Now about the times and the seasons, brothers and sisters, you have no need for anything to be written to you,
verse.note: The Greek plural was the ordinary way to address a mixed group of men and women, and the letter is plainly meant for the whole congregation (see verse 27). 'Brothers' alone now suggests to an English reader that only men are addressed. Several modern translations make the same choice; others keep 'brothers' with a footnote.

verse.text: for you yourselves know very well that the day of the Lord comes just like a thief in the night.
verse.note: The phrase comes from Israel's prophets (for example Amos 5 and Joel 2), where it names the day God acts decisively in judgment and rescue. Paul uses it for the coming of Jesus as Lord, which he has just described at the end of the previous chapter.

verse.text: When people are saying, “Peace and security,” then sudden destruction comes upon them, like labor pains upon a pregnant woman, and they will certainly not escape.
verse.note: Many scholars hear an echo of Roman imperial propaganda, which advertised peace and security as the benefits of Roman rule; Thessalonica was a city that prized its ties to Rome. Others see only an allusion to the false prophets who cried 'Peace' when there was no peace (Jeremiah 6:14). The two are not mutually exclusive, and the question remains debated.

verse.text: But you, brothers and sisters, are not in darkness, so that the day should overtake you like a thief,
for you are all children of light and children of the day. We do not belong to night or to darkness.

note.traditional: children of light / sons of light

verse.note: The Greek is literally 'sons of light and sons of day', a Semitic idiom in which 'son of X' means a person who belongs to X or is characterized by it. The expression 'sons of light' is known from Jewish writings of the period, including the Dead Sea Scrolls. 'Children' is used because the whole congregation is addressed.

verse.text: So then, let us not sleep as the rest do, but let us stay awake and be sober.
For those who sleep, sleep at night, and those who get drunk are drunk at night.
But since we belong to the day, let us be sober, having put on the breastplate of faith and love, and as a helmet the hope of salvation.

note.term: the breastplate of faith and love

verse.note: The image draws on Isaiah 59:17, where God himself puts on righteousness as a breastplate and a helmet of salvation. Paul applies the armor to believers and attaches to it his familiar triad of faith, love and hope.

verse.text: For God did not appoint us for wrath but to obtain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ,
who died for us so that, whether we are awake or asleep, we may live together with him.

note.term: whether we are awake or asleep

verse.note: These are the same two verbs used in verses 6–7 for moral alertness and moral stupor, but most interpreters take them here to mean 'alive or dead' at the Lord's coming, picking up the concern of 4:13–18 about believers who have died. A minority reads the words in the same moral sense as in verse 6, which sits awkwardly with the exhortation there. The translation keeps the same English words so the reader can see the echo.

verse.text: Therefore encourage one another and build each other up, just as you are in fact doing.
Now we ask you, brothers and sisters, to recognize those who labor among you and lead you in the Lord and admonish you,
verse.note: The Greek verb can mean either 'stand at the head of, lead' or 'care for, give aid to', and both senses are well attested in the period. Standing between 'labor' and 'admonish', it may describe practical care and patronage as much as authority; some translations render it 'care for you'. No formal office is named.

verse.text: and to hold them in the very highest regard in love because of their work. Be at peace among yourselves.
And we urge you, brothers and sisters: admonish the disorderly, comfort the fainthearted, help the weak, be patient with everyone.
verse.note: The word means 'out of order, undisciplined', used for example of soldiers who break ranks. Many modern versions translate 'idle' because 2 Thessalonians 3:6–11 uses related words of people who refuse to work, and some papyri use the word group for absence from work. The word itself is broader than laziness, however, so the general sense is kept here; older English versions had 'unruly'.

verse.text: See that no one repays anyone evil for evil, but always pursue what is good, both for one another and for everyone.
Rejoice always,
pray without ceasing,
give thanks in everything; for this is God’s will for you in Christ Jesus.
Do not quench the Spirit,
do not treat prophecies with contempt,
but test everything; hold on to what is good,
hold back from every kind of evil.
verse.note: The Greek noun can mean either 'outward appearance' or 'kind, sort'. The King James Version took the first sense ('abstain from all appearance of evil'), which has often been understood as avoiding anything that merely looks wrong. Most scholars and modern translations take it as 'kind' or 'form', which fits the contrast with 'what is good' in the previous verse. The two commands use related verbs in Greek, reflected here in 'hold on to' and 'hold back from'.

verse.text: Now may the God of peace himself make you holy through and through, and may your spirit and soul and body be kept whole and without blame at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.
verse.note: The Greek word means both arrival and presence, and in the period it was a standard term for the official visit of a king or emperor to a city. Readers in Thessalonica would have heard that overtone when it was used of the Lord Jesus.

verse.text: The one who calls you is faithful, and he will do it.
Brothers and sisters, pray for us.
Greet all the brothers and sisters with a holy kiss.
I put you under oath before the Lord to have this letter read to all the brothers and sisters.

note.term: I put you under oath before the Lord
note.traditional: I charge you by the Lord / I adjure you by the Lord

verse.note: The letter shifts here from 'we' to 'I', which suggests Paul adding a closing line in his own person. The verb is a strong one, binding the recipients by oath with the Lord as witness. Letters were read aloud to the gathered congregation, and Paul insists that no one be left out.

verse.text: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.
